name: return-address
intent: Let a requester embed the address of the channel where the answer should be delivered in the request itself, so a replier can respond to any caller without knowing who they are, where they are, or which of many clients is waiting.
problem: In request-reply messaging the replier must send its answer somewhere, yet it usually cannot know where: requesters are anonymous, ephemeral, behind NAT or a firewall, or simply one of many clients. Hard-coding a reply destination per caller couples the service to its callers and breaks as soon as a reply has to go somewhere else than the sender's usual inbound channel.
context: Request-reply over a message broker or message-capable transport (AMQP, JMS, NATS, MQTT 5, ZeroMQ, socket and callback protocols), where requests and replies travel on different channels and the requester's inbound address is either dynamic (temporary or exclusive queue, inbox subject, socket id, ack slot) or private and therefore not derivable by the replier. The same decision appears inside a process whenever an asynchronous request value must carry its own reply handle.
benefits: New requesters need no change in the replier: the reply destination is per request, so the service keeps no per-client routing table or configuration.
Reply routing becomes per request instead of per sender, so one service can answer the original caller, an aggregator, or a gateway that owns the real client connection.

The requester can use an ephemeral, private or firewalled address (temporary queue, inbox subject, connection-scoped callback) that the broker can still deliver to although the replier could never have guessed it.
Address metadata stays out of the payload: the body keeps its Document or Command Message contract while transport information rides in a header.
Composes with asynchronous and fan-in topologies: replies converge on the component that must correlate them rather than on the network node that happened to send the request.
tradeoffs: The return address is attacker-influenced routing data: honouring an unvalidated replyTo is an open-relay / SSRF class of defect and enables reply spoofing, so destinations must be allowlisted or derived from trusted identity.

A stale address fails silently: when the requester's temporary queue or connection is gone the reply is dropped with no bounce, which makes Message Expiration and a requester-side timeout load-bearing rather than optional.
Per-request reply channels cost broker resources and lifecycle management (declare, consume, delete, handle collisions), which is exactly why brokers added direct reply-to pseudo queues.
The address leaks infrastructure detail (queue and subject names, internal hostnames, tenant ids) to every consumer of the request and ties the message contract to one broker's addressing scheme.
An address identifies a destination, not a request: on any shared reply channel a Correlation Identifier is still required, so the pattern adds a header without removing the correlation burden.

participants.responsibility: Chooses or creates the reply channel, writes its address into the request's metadata, and consumes replies from that address.
Carries the return address as transport metadata beside the payload, so the reply destination travels with the data it belongs to.
The destination the replier can publish to without knowing the requester: a temporary queue, inbox subject, response topic, ack slot or in-process reply handle.
Reads the address from the incoming request and publishes the response there; it needs no prior knowledge of the requester and normally never learns its identity.
The answer, addressed to the return address and carrying the correlation metadata the requester needs to match it to the original request.
Resolves the address and enforces whether the replier may publish to it; it may refuse, dead-letter or silently drop the reply.

use_cases: RPC over RabbitMQ, NATS or JMS: the client declares an exclusive callback queue (or uses a direct reply-to pseudo queue) and workers answer to the address carried by the request.
Scatter-gather: every sub-request carries the aggregator's reply channel so partial results converge on the component that joined the fan-out.
A messaging gateway in front of a synchronous client (HTTP, WebSocket): the gateway puts its inbound connection's reply slot into the request so the far side can answer asynchronously.
Mobile and IoT devices behind NAT with short-lived connections: the request names a response topic, inbox or device shadow address instead of the device's unreachable socket address.
Serverless and edge functions that must answer into a still-open callback URL, WebSocket or ack slot rather than to a fixed queue.
Per-tenant or per-request isolation where each request gets its own reply channel that can be firewalled, metered and expired independently.

NATS Core request-reply: the client subscribes to a unique inbox subject, carries that subject as the request's reply address, and the service publishes its response there; request() adds timeout and no-responders handling.

MQTT 5 request/response as documented by RabbitMQ: the requester subscribes to a Response Topic and sends it with the request, while the responder publishes the reply there and echoes Correlation Data.
avoid_when: The reply path is fixed and known (one dedicated reply channel per pair): the header then adds a trust problem and no flexibility.
The transport already is the return address: an HTTP response, a gRPC stream, a method return value or a Future needs no addressing at all.
The broker offers a direct reply-to or auto-subscribed inbox mechanism (RabbitMQ amq.rabbitmq.reply-to, NATS inbox): prefer the pseudo or dynamic address over a hand-managed queue.
The requester is anonymous and untrusted and the broker cannot constrain destinations: answer on a channel you control instead of trusting the header.
The exchange is local and synchronous: a callback closure, continuation or channel inside the request value is the simpler equivalent.
anti_patterns: Blind relay: publishing to whatever replyTo says with no validation, turning the service into a message amplifier and SSRF pivot.
Address in the body: stuffing the reply destination into the payload instead of a header, so every consumer's data contract is polluted with transport metadata.
One global reply queue without correlation: all clients consume the same queue, replies cross-deliver, and the wrong consumer silently discards messages.
Leaking broker URIs with credentials or internal hostnames inside the address field.
Fire-and-forget return addresses: temporary reply queues that are never consumed, deleted or expired, accumulating broker state after every crash.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: transport routing metadata belongs in headers, application data in the payload.
Inversion of control: the replier depends on the message contract (it reads the address), never on a registry of callers.
Principle of least knowledge: publishing one's own address is cheaper than teaching the replier every requester's location.
Fail-safe defaults: treat the return address as untrusted input — if it cannot be validated, do not route to it.
Explicit failure handling: asynchronous replies need timeouts, expiry and dead-lettering to make the silent-drop case visible.
best_practices: Reuse the transport's native property (AMQP reply-to, JMS JMSReplyTo, MQTT 5 Response Topic, NATS reply subject) instead of inventing an application header.
Pair every return address with a correlation identifier and a message expiry, and honour both on the consuming side.
Validate and normalize the address against an allowlist of destinations you control before publishing a reply.
Prefer broker-managed ephemeral addresses (exclusive server-named queues, direct reply-to, auto-declared inboxes) so the address dies with the requester's session.
Document the reply channel's lifecycle — who declares it, who deletes it, what happens when the requester vanishes — and reap clients that never collect replies.
Log the reply destination together with the correlation id, but never log credentials or full broker URIs.
sources: Hohpe, G. and Woolf, B. (2003). Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions. Addison-Wesley — 'Message Construction': Return Address.
